resources.string: Share of total CPU time spent busy across the device during the interval between two readings.
Percent, 0–100. Calculated from changes in /proc/stat counters; idle and I/O wait are excluded from busy time.
Sustained high utilization can leave less execution time for other tasks, increasing response times and heat.
Compare sustained load with CPU wait, probe delay and thermal status. A short peak can be normal. A low device average can hide one saturated core.
An 80% reading means 80% of the aggregate counted CPU time was busy in this interval; it is not the agent process share.
Android may deny /proc/stat. Missing readings remain unavailable. CPU wait and probe delay then provide separate clues; they cannot reconstruct this percentage.
Feeds CPU pressure. Default thresholds are 80%, 90%, 95%, with time windows before changing the severity. Session settings may differ.
Device CPU counters: /proc/stat. Two valid readings are needed after start or reset.
Time that the dedicated probe thread was ready to execute but waited in the CPU run queue between two probes.
Milliseconds accumulated over the measured interval. Difference of the thread scheduler wait counters, converted from nanoseconds.
An increase suggests this thread had difficulty getting CPU time. Similar contention may delay application tasks, but other threads can behave differently.
Compare intervals of similar duration and look for repeated increases together with probe delay. Zero is valid; no universal warning threshold is assigned.
20 ms over a 2000 ms probe interval means this thread accumulated 20 ms waiting to run. It does not mean the whole device was 1% overloaded.

Only the agent probe thread is observed. Scheduling policy and other work affect it. A denied or inactive scheduler counter cannot prove absence of contention. Pauses, sleep and resets break the interval.
Does not affect CPU pressure or the overall performance state. It remains a separate indirect signal even if system CPU is available.
Probe thread: /proc/self/task/<tid>/schedstat, second counter. Availability is tested inside the APK.
How late the probe thread actually starts compared with its scheduled execution time.
Milliseconds of lateness per probe, measured with monotonic uptime. This is a scheduling delay, not application startup duration.
Repeated delays can accompany poor responsiveness when work cannot run on time.
Look for repeated peaks and compare them with CPU wait and thermal status. Small delays are expected; the value alone does not identify a bottleneck.
A probe planned for uptime 5000 ms that begins at 5025 ms has a delay of 25 ms.

CPU competition, garbage collection and Android scheduling restrictions can contribute. Deep sleep is excluded by resetting the baseline; unavailable or stale probes are omitted. No universal normal threshold is defined.
Does not affect CPU pressure or the overall performance state. It can remain available when /proc counters are denied.
Dedicated probe thread and monotonic uptime timer. Each reading uses the probe timestamp rather than the later database write time.
Total RAM available to the operating system on this device.
Bytes; displayed as MiB or GiB. 1 MiB = 1048576 bytes. Read from Android totalMem.
Provides the capacity against which available memory is assessed; lower capacity leaves less room for simultaneous tasks.
Usually stable. Interpret available bytes together with this total rather than comparing raw free amounts across different phones.
On a device reporting 1024 MiB total and 128 MiB available, available memory is 12.5%.
This is system RAM, not app heap size or storage capacity. Hardware reservations can make it smaller than the marketed RAM figure. It does not identify memory consumers.
Used as the denominator of available memory percentage, which feeds memory pressure. Total size alone does not set severity.
Device memory: ActivityManager.getMemoryInfo(), MemoryInfo.totalMem.
RAM that Android currently considers available for new work.
Bytes, shown as MiB or GiB; sampled from availMem at each collection.
A sustained decline can reduce room for new allocations and accompany reclamation, application restarts or delayed work.
Compare with total RAM, available percentage and the low-memory flag. A decrease after starting apps can be normal; a repeating decline deserves investigation.
128 MiB available on a 1024 MiB device equals 12.5%; the same 128 MiB on a larger device is a smaller fraction.
This is not simply unused physical memory and not the free heap of one app. Android manages caches; this value alone neither proves a leak nor guarantees an allocation will succeed.
Used to calculate available memory percentage. Memory pressure also considers the Android low-memory flag.
Device memory: ActivityManager.getMemoryInfo(), MemoryInfo.availMem.
Fraction of total RAM currently reported as available by Android.
Percent, 0–100: available bytes divided by total bytes, multiplied by 100.
A low sustained percentage can indicate limited room for concurrent applications and new allocations.
Lower values mean less available capacity. Default pressure boundaries are 15%, 10%, 5%; these are app defaults, not universal device limits.
128 MiB available out of 1024 MiB gives 12.5%, in the default warning band before time-window filtering.
Interpret with the low-memory flag and absolute bytes. Cache management and device workload matter. A short dip does not prove a memory leak.
Feeds memory pressure with descending thresholds. Android low-memory=true requests a critical raw level; the configured time windows still apply.
Derived from MemoryInfo.availMem / totalMem. Session thresholds can differ from current settings.
Android flag indicating that the device is currently in a low-memory condition.
A flag: 0 = no low-memory signal, 1 = low-memory signal. It is not a byte count or percentage.
A value of 1 is a system warning that memory is constrained and background work may be affected.
Treat repeated 1 values as a strong signal to inspect available RAM and application behavior. Zero does not guarantee that every app has enough heap space.
With low-memory=1, the raw memory severity is critical even if the configured available-percent thresholds would produce a lower level.
This follows the Android decision, which can vary by device and software version. It does not identify a leaking or terminated application.
Forces the raw memory pressure candidate to critical; configured escalation and recovery windows still apply, so the displayed level need not change immediately.
Device memory: ActivityManager.getMemoryInfo(), MemoryInfo.lowMemory.
Memory threshold reported by Android for its low-memory assessment.
Bytes, displayed as MiB or GiB. This is the system threshold, not an editable AHWOTel percentage boundary.
Helps explain the low-memory flag and how much absolute memory Android considers a small reserve.
Compare available memory with this threshold and the actual low-memory flag. The threshold provides context rather than a separate diagnosis.
Available RAM of 80 MiB against a reported threshold of 100 MiB suggests a small reserve; check the system flag too.
Device policy can differ. Do not assume this threshold equals 5%, 10% or 15% of RAM, or use it to predict the exact next process termination.
Shown as diagnostic context only. AHWOTel uses available percentage and the Android low-memory flag for memory pressure, not a direct comparison with this field.
Device memory: ActivityManager.getMemoryInfo(), MemoryInfo.threshold.
Total size of the filesystem containing the private app data directory.
Bytes, shown as MiB or GiB. Read from StatFs.totalBytes for the app files directory.
Sets the capacity against which the remaining storage reserve is assessed.
Usually stable. Compare available bytes and percentage on this same filesystem; a capacity change may reflect a different mount or device setup.
If this filesystem has 16 GiB total and 4 GiB available, its available fraction is 25%.
This is not the size of AHWOTel data, all device disks combined, or necessarily the marketed storage capacity. Other apps can share this filesystem.
Used as the denominator of storage available percentage. Capacity alone does not set storage pressure.
App data filesystem: StatFs(context.filesDir), totalBytes.
Free space that ordinary applications can use on the filesystem containing AHWOTel data.
Bytes, displayed as MiB or GiB; sampled from StatFs.availableBytes.
A small reserve can prevent writes, downloads or database growth and affect applications sharing the partition.
Watch sustained decreases and compare with total capacity and available percentage. An increase can follow cleanup by any app.
2 GiB available on a 16 GiB filesystem gives 12.5% remaining capacity.
Filesystem reserves are excluded. This is not the app history quota and does not guarantee that every write succeeds; app or system limits may apply.
Used to calculate storage available percentage, which feeds storage pressure. AHWOTel history size is reported separately in Diagnostics.
App data filesystem: StatFs(context.filesDir), availableBytes.
Filesystem capacity that is not available to ordinary applications, calculated as total minus available bytes.
Bytes, displayed as MiB or GiB. Includes occupied space and capacity reserved from ordinary applications.
Growth reduces available reserve and can eventually interfere with writes or updates on the shared filesystem.
Read alongside available percentage. This measurement cannot attribute growth to AHWOTel or any other individual app.
For 16 GiB total and 4 GiB available, this calculated value is 12 GiB.
It is not a directory size and not exactly the sum of user file sizes because reserved capacity is included. Diagnostics reports AHWOTel storage separately.
No separate threshold is applied to this field. Storage pressure uses available percentage instead.
Derived from StatFs.totalBytes − StatFs.availableBytes on the app data filesystem.
Percentage of the app data filesystem capacity available to ordinary applications.
Percent, 0–100: available bytes / total bytes × 100.
A low reserve can affect writes, updates and applications using the same filesystem.
Lower is more constrained. Default pressure thresholds are 15%, 10%, 5%; compare with absolute free bytes and expected data growth.
2 GiB available out of 16 GiB is 12.5%, in the default warning band before time filtering.
These thresholds are configurable application defaults, not universal filesystem failure points. Available capacity does not measure storage speed or I/O latency.
Feeds storage pressure using descending thresholds and the configured escalation/recovery windows.
Derived from StatFs.availableBytes and totalBytes for the app data filesystem.
Android thermal throttling status for the device, rather than a temperature in degrees.
Codes: 0 none, 1 light, 2 moderate, 3 severe, 4 critical, 5 emergency, 6 shutdown.
Higher levels indicate stronger heat-related restrictions, which can reduce CPU/GPU performance and delay work.
Look for sustained increases and slower task execution at the same time. The numeric gaps are category steps, not equal temperature differences.
Status 3 means Android reports severe throttling. It does not mean 3 degrees or 3% load.
Requires Android API 29 and device support. The manufacturer defines sensor and policy behavior; this does not identify one specific hot component. Compare with headroom and battery temperature.
Feeds thermal pressure. Default boundaries are statuses 1, 2, 3, followed by the configured time windows; Android thermal codes and app severity codes are different scales.
Device thermal policy: PowerManager.currentThermalStatus.
Android estimate of how much of the thermal envelope is currently in use. Despite the name, a larger value means closer to severe throttling, not more spare capacity.
Dimensionless value. 1.0 is the severe-throttling reference; values can exceed 1.0. AHWOTel requests the current estimate, without forecasting.
An upward trend can help explain heat-related performance reduction.
Compare the trend with thermal status. Zero is not a temperature; 0.5 does not promise half the CPU performance remains. Values above 1 have no fixed mapping to higher status codes.
A rise from 0.7 to 0.95 moves closer to the 1.0 severe reference; it does not mean that 95% of CPU is busy.

Requires API 30 and device support. Polled no more frequently than once every 10 seconds; the actual frequency depends on the sampling interval. Gaps between readings are expected. Unsupported or non-finite values are unavailable; this is not a direct CPU sensor.
Informational only; does not affect thermal pressure or overall state. Those use the thermal status code.
Device estimate: PowerManager.getThermalHeadroom(0), sampled no more often than every 10 seconds.
Remaining battery charge reported by Android as a fraction of its reported full-charge scale.
Percent, 0–100: level / scale × 100, read from the battery broadcast.
A decreasing level reflects use of the available charge and helps assess whether a long task can continue on battery.
Compare the slope over similar workloads and check charging state. A single reading is not a measurement of power draw or remaining runtime.
A change from 80% to 75% is a decrease of 5 percentage points; it does not determine watts consumed by the agent.
Charge estimates can be coarse and device-dependent. USB power changes the experiment; this metric alone cannot attribute consumption to one app or measure battery health.
Informational only; does not affect the overall performance state.
Device battery: ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED, EXTRA_LEVEL and EXTRA_SCALE.
Whether the Android battery status is charging or full, grouped into one flag by AHWOTel.
0 = another reported battery status; 1 = charging or full. Missing status produces no value.
Provides context for charge level and temperature: external power can change both the battery trend and device heating.
Use this flag when comparing sessions on battery and while plugged in. One does not necessarily mean current is flowing into the battery at that instant.
A full battery produces 1 even when its level stays at 100%.
The flag does not report charging current, charger power or cable type. Android unknown/not-charging/discharging statuses map to 0 in this implementation.
Informational only; does not affect the overall performance state.
Device battery: ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED, EXTRA_STATUS; CHARGING and FULL map to 1.
Battery temperature reported by Android. This is a battery reading, not CPU temperature.
Degrees Celsius. The reported integer in tenths of a degree is divided by 10.
Rising battery temperature can accompany charging, workload or a warm environment and help explain thermal behavior.
Compare trends under similar conditions with charging and thermal status. Limits depend on the device; this app assigns no universal battery-temperature alarm threshold.
A reported raw value of 350 becomes 35 °C. This example is a conversion, not a recommended operating limit.
Sensor availability and accuracy depend on the device. Battery temperature can differ from CPU and surface temperatures; it does not prove the cause of a thermal restriction.
Informational only; does not affect thermal pressure or overall state. Thermal pressure uses the Android thermal status.
Device battery: ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED, EXTRA_TEMPERATURE / 10.
Filtered assessment of CPU constraints derived from CPU utilization.
Ordinal code: 0 normal, 1 warning, 2 degraded, 3 critical. These codes are not percentages or physical measurements.
A sustained higher level highlights CPU conditions that may interfere with responsive or reliable task execution.
Default boundaries: 80%, 90%, 95%. A higher candidate must persist for 30 seconds and recovery for 60 seconds by default. A changing candidate restarts its window.
With default settings, 92% gives a raw degraded candidate. From normal, a steady candidate for at least 30 seconds is needed before displaying level 2.

Thresholds and windows are session settings. Gaps reset the filter; unavailable inputs yield no assessment. Initial normal can reflect a pending window. Historical sessions may use different settings.
Contributes to overall performance state as one of the available resource assessments. The overall value is their maximum.
Derived by AHWOTel PressureWindow from CPU utilization; not an Android severity code.
Filtered assessment of memory constraints derived from available RAM percentage and the low-memory flag.
Ordinal code: 0 normal, 1 warning, 2 degraded, 3 critical. These codes are not percentages or physical measurements.
A sustained higher level highlights memory conditions that may interfere with responsive or reliable task execution.

Default boundaries: 15%, 10%, 5% (descending). A higher candidate must persist for 30 seconds and recovery for 60 seconds by default. A changing candidate restarts its window. The Android low-memory flag requests a critical raw level, still subject to the time window.
With default settings, 8% available gives a raw degraded candidate. From normal, a steady candidate for at least 30 seconds is needed before displaying level 2.

Thresholds and windows are session settings. Gaps reset the filter; unavailable inputs yield no assessment. Initial normal can reflect a pending window. Historical sessions may use different settings.
Contributes to overall performance state as one of the available resource assessments. The overall value is their maximum.
Derived by AHWOTel PressureWindow from available RAM percentage and the low-memory flag; not an Android severity code.
Filtered assessment of storage constraints derived from available filesystem percentage.
Ordinal code: 0 normal, 1 warning, 2 degraded, 3 critical. These codes are not percentages or physical measurements.
A sustained higher level highlights storage conditions that may interfere with responsive or reliable task execution.
Default boundaries: 15%, 10%, 5% (descending). A higher candidate must persist for 30 seconds and recovery for 60 seconds by default. A changing candidate restarts its window.
With default settings, 8% available gives a raw degraded candidate. From normal, a steady candidate for at least 30 seconds is needed before displaying level 2.

Thresholds and windows are session settings. Gaps reset the filter; unavailable inputs yield no assessment. Initial normal can reflect a pending window. Historical sessions may use different settings.
Contributes to overall performance state as one of the available resource assessments. The overall value is their maximum.
Derived by AHWOTel PressureWindow from available filesystem percentage; not an Android severity code.
Filtered assessment of thermal constraints derived from Android thermal status.
Ordinal code: 0 normal, 1 warning, 2 degraded, 3 critical. These codes are not percentages or physical measurements.
A sustained higher level highlights thermal conditions that may interfere with responsive or reliable task execution.
Default boundaries: 1, 2, 3. A higher candidate must persist for 30 seconds and recovery for 60 seconds by default. A changing candidate restarts its window.
With default settings, status 2 gives a raw degraded candidate. From normal, a steady candidate for at least 30 seconds is needed before displaying level 2.

Thresholds and windows are session settings. Gaps reset the filter; unavailable inputs yield no assessment. Initial normal can reflect a pending window. Historical sessions may use different settings.
Contributes to overall performance state as one of the available resource assessments. The overall value is their maximum.
Derived by AHWOTel PressureWindow from Android thermal status; not an Android severity code.
Overall assessment formed from the worst available CPU, memory, storage and thermal pressure levels.
Ordinal code: 0 normal, 1 warning, 2 degraded, 3 critical. Maximum of available filtered resource levels; no value if none is available.
Helps locate periods when at least one monitored resource may constrain work, then directs investigation to that resource.
Open individual pressure charts to see what raised the state. Normal means no available assessment is currently elevated; it is not a guarantee that the device or an app is healthy.
If memory pressure is 2, storage is 0 and CPU/thermal are unavailable, overall state is 2 from a partial assessment.

Missing resources are excluded, not treated as proven normal. Indirect CPU signals, battery and headroom are excluded. Resource windows delay changes; the result is not a causal diagnosis or an app response-time measurement.
This is the final state. It takes the maximum after each resource has applied its own escalation/recovery window; no second global time window is added.
Derived by AHWOTel from CPU_PRESSURE, MEMORY_PRESSURE, STORAGE_PRESSURE and THERMAL_PRESSURE.
